## Introduction

This is the hands-on continuation of today's lecture on version control with Git.

### Learning goals for this lecture

- Learn the basic Git workflow and the most common Git commands.
- Make Git ignore specific files and dirs.
- Undo accidental changes to your files.
- Show the changes you've made to files, also using VS Code's Git interface.

## One-time Git configuration

We will start with one-time personal Git configuration.
This will apply anywhere on OSC,
and won't ever have to be redone unless you want to make changes.

These steps are all done with `git config --global`:

1. Make your **name** known to Git,
   since it will be recorded in every commit you make ---
   your actual first and last name (***not** your OSC or GitHub username!*):

   ```sh
   git config --global user.name "John Doe"
   ```

2. Make your **email** address known
   (_should match the address associated with your GitHub account,_
   _if you already created one_):

   ```sh
   git config --global user.email "doe.391@osu.edu"
   ```

3. Set a default **text editor** for Git.
   (Git may occasionally open a text editor for you.
   Even though we're using VS Code,
   here it is better to select a text editor that runs in the shell, like `nano`^[
   Git will open an editor when you need to provide a "commit message" but didn't
   enter one on the command line.
   Its default editor is `vi`/`vim`, which is harder to use and
   notoriously hard for beginners to exit.].)

   ```sh
   git config --global core.editor "nano -w"
   ```

4. Change the default "**branch**" name to `main`
   (Git's default is still the older `master`, whereas GitHub uses `main`)^[
    We'll talk a bit about what branches are later on.]:

   ```sh
   git config --global init.defaultBranch main
   ```

5. Finally, **print** your current settings to check whether you successfully changed them:

   ```sh
   git config --global --list
   ```
   ```bash-out
   user.name=John Doe
   user.email=doe.391@osu.edu
   core.editor=nano -w
   init.defaultbranch=main
   ```

## The basic Git workflow

You'll create a Git repository for a **mock book project**:
writing Charles Darwin's "On the Origin of Species".
This example follows Chapter 2 of @allesina2019.
The topic may seem silly, but keeping the content trivial means you can focus
entirely on the Git workflow.

### Create and move to a new project dir

Create a new dir for a mock project that you will version-control with Git:

``` sh
# (Your starting point should be /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER)
mkdir -p week05/evo
cd week05/evo
```

Next, we'll open this dir in VS Code with "**Open Folder**" to move all of VS Code,
not just the terminal, to this dir.
For example, after moving, the file explorer will only show this project's files,
and VS Code's Git functionality will work with the repo you'll create here.
(This is also how you'll want to work with your own projects:
open each project's dir as the folder in VS Code.)

1. Click {{< fa bars >}} &rarr; `File` &rarr; `Open Folder`.
2. Type/select `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/week05/evo`,
   replacing `<user>` with your user name.
   _This will cause VS Code to reload._
3. Open a new terminal and check that you are in the `evo` dir:

   ```sh
   pwd
   ```
   ```bash-out
   /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/week05/evo
   ```

### Start a new Git repository

Now we're ready to start your first Git repository!
The command to **initialize a new Git repository is `git init`** ---
use that to start a repo for the `evo` dir:

``` sh
git init
```
``` bash-out
Initialized empty Git repository in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/week05/evo/.git/
```

Can you confirm that this hidden dir is there?
The `ls` command will show hidden files and dirs with the `-a` option,
and indeed, the `.git` dir is present:

```bash
# (ls -a will also show the current dir "." and the parent dir "..")
ls -a
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="ls-blue">.</span>  <span class="ls-blue">..</span>  <span class="ls-blue">.git</span></code></pre>

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### Where (not) to run `git init` _(Click to expand)_
Above, we created a Git repo in an empty dir,
but you can use `git init` just the same in a dir that already contains files.
However, only run it in the top-level dir of a single project, and never:

- In a dir like your home dir or `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`,
  which contains many projects,
- Inside a dir that is already part of a Git repo.

If you did run `git init` in the wrong place,
you can undo it by removing the `.git` dir that it created using `rm -rf .git`^[
`-f` is needed because some files inside `.git` are write-protected ---
and recall from last week that `rm -rf` is unforgiving, so double-check
that you are removing the correct `.git` dir!].
:::

Next, check the status of your new repository with `git status`:

``` sh
git status
```

``` bash-out
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
```

Git reports that you:

- Are on a "**branch**" called `main`.
  We won't cover Git branches in class, but this is discussed in the
  [optional self-study material](../bonus/git.qmd) and in @allesina2019 Chapter 2.6.
  Basically, branches are "parallel versions" of your repository that are useful
  for collaborative and experimental work.
- Have not created any commits yet.
- Have "nothing to commit" because there are no files in this dir.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### The "not a git repository" error _(Click to expand)_

If you run a Git command, like `git status`,
outside of an existing Git repository, you'll get this error:

```bash-out-solo
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
```

That usually just means that you're in the wrong dir: check with `pwd`.
The bigger point is that Git commands only work inside a Git repository,
not in any other directory.
:::

### Your first Git commit

Start writing the book ([😉]{style="font-size:1.2em"})
by `echo`-ing text into a new file called `origin.txt`:

``` sh
echo "An essay on ..." > origin.txt
```

Now, check the status of the repository again:

``` sh
git status
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">origin.txt</span>

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)</code></pre>

Git has clearly **detected** the new file.
But as mentioned in the intro slides, Git does not automatically start "tracking" files ---
that is, it won't automatically include all files that are in your dir in the repository.
Instead, it tells you the file is "Untracked" and gives a hint on how to add it to the repository.

Start **tracking** the file and **stage** it in one go with `git add`:

``` sh
git add origin.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
As always, Tab-complete file names, like `origin.txt` above!
:::

Next, check the status of the repo again:

``` sh
git status
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached &lt;file&gt;..." to unstage)
        <span class="git-green">new file:   origin.txt</span></code></pre>

Now, your file has been added to the **staging area** (also called the **Index**)
and is listed as a "_change to be committed_"^[
You also get a hint on how to "*unstage*" the file:
i.e., reverting what you just did with `git add` and leaving the file untracked once again].
That phrase means that if you now run `git commit`,
the file will be included in that commit.

So, with your file tracked & staged, let's make your **first commit**.
Add the option `-m` followed by a "**commit message**":
a short description of the changes you are including in the current commit^[
If you leave out `-m`, Git will instead open the `nano` editor that you
configured above, so you can type your commit message there.
Type your message, then press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>X</kbd>, <kbd>Y</kbd> (to save),
and <kbd>Enter</kbd> (to confirm the file name) --- Git will then make the commit.]:

``` sh
git commit -m "Started the book"
```

``` bash-out
[main (root-commit) 3df4361] Started the book
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 origin.txt
```

You've made your first commit!
Here is another way of visualizing how changes are staged and committed in Git ---
and of the three areas that files can be in:

1. The **working tree** (also called working dir) is where you make changes to files.
2. The **staging area** (also called **Index**) is where you stage changes to be included in the next commit.
3. The **commit history** is where committed changes are stored.
   It has many "layers" of commits, and you can go back to any of them at any time.

![](/img/git-do2.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" .no-border fig-alt="A diagram of the process of adding and committing changes with Git commands" .lightbox}

::: legend2
Note that `git add` has a dual function: it starts tracking files and stages them.
:::

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>Why might the term "working tree" be used instead of "working directory"? *(Click to see the answer)*</summary>

The term "working tree" is used in Git to emphasize that we are referring to the
entire hierarchy of dirs and files that makes up your project,
and not the single dir that your terminal is currently in.

That said, both terms are often used interchangeably.
As such, if you hear "working dir" **in a Git context**,
it usually refers to the entire hierarchy.

</details>

### Checking the status and history

First, let's check the status of the repo again:

``` sh
git status
```

``` bash-out
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

It reported "nothing to commit, working tree clean",
which means no changes have been made anywhere in the project dir since the last commit.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Try to get in the habit of using `git status` a lot ---
as a sanity check before and after other `git` actions.
:::

Next, look at the **commit history** of the repo with `git log`:

``` sh
git log
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-yellow">commit 3df4361c1de9b71e08bf6e050105d53097acec21</span> (<span class="git-cyan git-bold">HEAD</span> -&gt; <span class="git-green git-bold">main</span>)
Author: Jelmer Poelstra &lt;jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com&gt;
Date:   Mon Mar 11 10:55:35 2024 -0400

    Started the book</code></pre>

Notes on the first line of the above output:

- The long "hexadecimal code" (which uses numbers and the letters `a`–`f`)
  is a unique identifier for that commit, usually called the **commit hash**
  (or SHA-1 checksum).
  You can reference and access each past commit by its hash,
  and the first 7 characters are usually enough
  (as you'll see with `git log --oneline` below).

- `(HEAD -> main)` means that you are (your "HEAD" is) currently located at
  the commit in question, and that the commit was made on the `main` branch.

Below that, `git log` reports the author, date and time of the commit,
and the commit message you provided.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: Put the commands in order

Say you want to start a brand-new project with a Git repository,
and make a first commit containing a single file, `notes.md`.
In which order should you run the commands below?
_(Only figure out the order --- don't run these commands.)_

```{.bash code-line-numbers="true"}
git commit -m "Start notes"
git init
cd myproject
git add notes.md
echo "# Project notes" > notes.md
mkdir myproject
```

<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

```bash
mkdir myproject
cd myproject
git init
echo "# Project notes" > notes.md
git add notes.md
git commit -m "Start notes"
```

</details>

_Bonus_: two of these commands could be swapped without any problems.
Which ones?

<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

`git init` and `echo` can be swapped:
Git doesn't care whether files already existed when you initialized the repo!
Swapping `git add` and `git commit`, on the other hand,
would make Git report that there is nothing to commit.

</details>

:::

On the Origin of Species

Check the status of the repo:

``` sh

```

<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore &lt;file&gt;..." to discard changes in working directory)

Git has **noticed** the changes, because the file is being tracked:

But changes to tracked files are **not** automatically staged.
Use `git add` to **stage** the file as a first step to committing these changes:

``` sh
git add origin.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Git never acts on files by itself
Git behaves similarly when it comes to new files and changes to tracked files:
it does not automatically do anything with them.
That is deliberate: managing which files are tracked and staged is up to you.
:::

Now, make your second commit, again adding a commit message.
Like always, it's up to you to decide what to write,
but the idea is that you give a short description of the changes you made:

``` sh

```

``` bash-out
[main f106353] Changed the title as suggested by Murray

```

Git gives a brief summary of the changes that were made:
you changed 1 file (`origin.txt`), and since you replaced the line of text in that file,
it interprets that as 1 insertion (the new line) and 1 deletion (the replaced line).

Check the history of the repo again --- you'll see that there are now 2 commits:

Date:   Mon Mar 11 10:55:35 2024 -0400

    Started the book</code></pre>

As you start accumulating commits,
you might prefer `git log --oneline` for a one-line-per-commit summary:

```bash
git log --oneline
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-yellow">f106353</span> (<span class="git-cyan git-bold">HEAD</span> -&gt; <span class="git-green git-bold">main</span>) Changed the title as suggested by Murray
<span class="git-yellow">3df4361</span> Started the book</code></pre>

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### When `git log` output is longer than your screen _(Click to expand)_
Once your history is longer than your screen,
`git log` opens in the `less` pager that you used last week:
scroll with the arrow keys and press <kbd>q</kbd> to get back to your prompt.
The same goes for long `git diff` output.
:::

::: {#commit-am .callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Staging multiple files at once, and `git commit -a` _(Click to expand)_

When you would like to stage multiple files, you don't need to add them one-by-one.
Here are a few other options:

- Stage **all files** in the project/repository:

  ``` sh
  # [Don't run any of this - these are hypothetical examples]
  git add --all
  ```

- Stage all files in the **current dir and its subdirs**
  (when run from the repo's root dir, this is the same as `git add --all`):

  ```sh
  git add .
  ```

- Stage all files in a **specific dir** (here: 'scripts') in the project:

  ```sh
  git add scripts/
  ```

Finally, you can **stage and commit all changes** with a single command
using the `-a` option for `git commit`
(but be aware that this will not add untracked files):

``` sh
git commit -am "My commit message"
```
:::

### What to include in individual commits

As shown in the box above, there's a way to stage and commit all changes to tracked
files at once.
That may seem more convenient than separately `git add`ing files before committing.
However, we focus on the more deliberate workflow of staging and committing files separately,
because it encourages you to think about what changes you are committing.

Rather than committing lots of things at once (say, at the end of each day),
it's good practice to make each commit a unit of progress worth saving ---
and as such, to **create separate commits for distinct changes**, even if those are small.

For example, say you use `git status` and find that since your last commit you have:

- Updated a README file to include more information about your samples.
- Worked on a script to run quality control of sequence files.

These are unrelated changes, and it's **not** recommended to include both in a single commit.

::: exercise

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Separate commits?

Say that since your last commit, you have changed three files:

1. `README.md`: you added information about your samples.
2. `scripts/qc.sh`: you changed the output dir of this QC script from `qc` to `results/qc`.
3. `scripts/qc_summary.sh`: you changed the dir that this script reads QC results from,
   also from `qc` to `results/qc`.

How many commits would you make, and which file(s) would go in each?

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

Two commits: one with `README.md`, and one with both scripts.

The changes to the two scripts are in different files,
but they form a single unit of progress:
if you committed only the change to `qc.sh`,
that commit would contain a `qc_summary.sh` script that looks for QC results in the wrong place.
So, the rule is "one commit per change", not "one commit per file".
</details>
---->

:::

You have now learned the basic Git workflow! 🥳
Below, we'll go through a few related key aspects of using Git.

## Ignoring files and directories

As discussed in the [intro slides](./w5a_git-intro.qmd#what-to-version-control),
it's best not to track some files,
such as (bulky) data files, temporary files, and results.
At the same time, we've seen that Git reports any "untracked" files in your project
whenever you run `git status`.

Having these files reported every time you run `git status` can get annoying and
make it harder to spot changes and untracked files that you _do_ want to add.
More importantly, it makes it easy to commit such files by accident ---
and once a large data file has been committed,
it stays in the repo's history even if you later delete it (!).

To deal with this, you can **tell Git not to pay attention to certain files** by
adding file names and wildcard selections to a special file called `.gitignore`.

As an example,
let's start by adding some types of content you would not want to commit
to your repository: a dir `data`, and a file ending in a `~`
(a type of backup file that some text editors create):

``` sh
mkdir data
touch data/drawings.png todo.txt~
```

Before checking what Git reports,
let's take a look at the current contents of our project dir with `tree`:

```sh
tree
```
```{=html}
<pre class="bash-out"><code>.
├── <span style="color: #0328fc;">data</span>
│   └── drawings.png
├── origin.txt
├── todo.txt
└── todo.txt~

1 directory, 4 files</code></pre>
```

When you check the status of the repo, you should see that Git has noticed the
new files:

``` sh
git status
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">data/</span>
        <span class="git-red">todo.txt~</span></code></pre>

::: callout-note
#### How untracked dirs are reported
When a dir is untracked, Git reports the dir name and does not list the files
inside it (above, the `drawings.png` file inside `data` is not shown).
That is helpful, because it avoids cluttering the output of `git status`,
but it's good to be aware of.
:::

You can create a `.gitignore` file to prevent Git from reporting these files
whenever you run `git status`:

- This is a plain text file that contains dir and file names/patterns,
  all of which will be ignored by Git.
- The file should be called `.gitignore` and be **placed in the project's root dir**
  (use one `.git` file per repo).

Some more things to know about `.gitignore`:

- As soon as a `.gitignore` file exists,
  Git automatically checks and processes its contents.
- Perhaps somewhat counterintuitively,
  you _should_ add and commit the `.gitignore` file itself
  (that way, it's shared along with the rest of the repo,
  such as with collaborators or on GitHub).

Create a `.gitignore` file and open it in the editor:

``` sh
# After this command, click on the file name in the file explorer to open it:
touch .gitignore
```

Then, type the following two lines in the file
(press <kbd>Enter</kbd> at the end of the last line too):

```{.file filename=".gitignore" .numberLines}
data/
*~


```

The first line makes Git ignore everything in the `data` dir,
and the second makes it ignore everything that ends in a `~`.
That is:

- `.gitignore` files accept the same **wildcard patterns** as the shell,
  so `*` matches any string of characters.

- But unlike wildcards in the shell, which only match files in the current dir,
  these patterns apply **across the entire repo**:
  `*~` will also match files ending in `~` in any subdir
  (and `data/` will match a `data` dir at any level).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### It doesn't matter _how_ you change files _(Click to expand)_
So far, you have been changing files with `echo`, but here you are using the editor.
Git doesn't care _how_ a file changed: it only looks at file contents.
In your own projects, you'll mostly edit files in the editor,
and then use the terminal to stage and commit your changes.
:::

When you check the status again,
you should see that Git has automatically processed the `.gitignore` file,
since the targeted files are no longer listed as untracked:

``` sh
git status
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">.gitignore</span></code></pre>

However, you do now have an untracked `.gitignore` file,
so track and commit this file as follows:

``` sh
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Added a gitignore file"
```

``` bash-out
[main 9715ab5] Added a gitignore file
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 4: `.gitignore`

1. Say that a repo's `.gitignore` file contains these two lines:

   ```bash-out-solo
   results/
   *.log
   ```

   Which of these new files would Git now ignore?

   a) `results/counts.tsv`
   b) `run.log`
   c) `scripts/run.log`
   d) `scripts/qc.sh`

   <!----
   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   It would ignore all except **d)**.
   `results/counts.tsv` is inside an ignored dir, and both `.log` files match `*.log`.
   Note that c) is ignored too: patterns like `*.log` (and `results/`, too)
   match in any dir of the repo, not just in the top-level dir.
   </details>
   ---->

2. _Bonus_: Say that you add "todo.txt" to the `.gitignore` file of your  `evo`
   repo, and then append another line to `todo.txt`.
   What do you think, would `git status` still report that `todo.txt` was modified?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   Yes, it would report that `todo.txt` was modified,
   because `.gitignore` only affects currently _untracked_ files.

   Since `todo.txt` is already tracked (you committed it in Exercise 3),
   Git keeps tracking it and reports changes to it.

   To **stop tracking a file**, you'd first have to remove it from the repo,
   as shown in the [optional self-study material for Git](../bonus/git.qmd).
   </details>
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-tip
#### Good project file organization makes ignoring files easier

If you keep your data and results in their own top-level dirs, as recommended in week 2,
the two lines `data/` and `results/` in your `.gitignore` file are all you need to ignore them.
If you instead mix, for example, scripts and results within dirs,
you'll need many more specific and error-prone `.gitignore` entries.
:::

## Undoing changes that have not been committed

Now, we'll practice undoing changes to your working tree
by recovering a version from the repo: in other words,
using Git as an "undo button" after accidental file changes or removal.
(In the [optional self-study Git material](../bonus/git.qmd),
you can learn how to unstage files and how to undo changes that _have_ been committed.)

Say you **accidentally overwrote** a file,
and want to recover the previous version from the repo:

1. Let's first check the contents of `todo.txt`:

   ```sh
   cat todo.txt
   ```
   ```bash-out
   June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
   ```

2. You accidentally overwrite the file contents instead of appending to it [😳]{style="font-size: 1.2em;"}:

   ```sh
   echo "Finish taxidermy of the finches" > todo.txt
   ```

3. Confirm the disaster by checking the file contents again:

   ```sh
   cat todo.txt
   ```
   ```bash-out
   Finish taxidermy of the finches
   ```

4. Always start by checking the status:

   ```sh
   git status
   ```
   <pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main
   Changes not staged for commit:
     (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to update what will be committed)
     (use "git restore &lt;file&gt;..." to discard changes in working directory)
           <span class="git-red">modified:   todo.txt</span>

   no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")</code></pre>

5. You'll want to "discard changes in working directory",
   and Git told you how to do this --- with `git restore`:

   ```sh
   git restore todo.txt
   ```

6. Check if it worked by looking at the file contents:

   ```sh
   cat todo.txt
   ```
   ```bash-out
   June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
   ```

Great! You have successfully recovered the previous version of the file from the repo.
If you **accidentally deleted a file**,
you can similarly retrieve it with `git restore`:

1. You accidentally remove `todo.txt`:

   ```sh
   rm todo.txt
   ```

2. Use `git restore` to get the file back!

   ```bash
   git restore todo.txt

   cat todo.txt
   ```
   ```bash-out
   June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
   ```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-warning}
#### git restore can only bring back what Git has stored
`git restore` replaces your file with the version stored by Git
(the last commit, or the staged version if you staged the file).
Had you not committed `todo.txt` in Exercise 3, its contents would now be gone for good.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### git restore itself cannot be undone _(Click to expand)_
`git restore` overwrites your current version of the file without asking for confirmation.
So be careful when using it: if the file contained changes that you had not committed,
those changes are gone for good --- Git cannot undo a `git restore`.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: What can Git restore?

In which of these situations can `git restore` get back what you lost?

a) You accidentally removed a new file that you had never added with `git add`.
b) You accidentally removed a whole dir of committed files with `rm -r`.
c) You had edited a committed file without staging or committing those edits,
   and then accidentally overwrote the file. You want those edits back.

<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

The only correct answer is **b**,
because Git can only restore versions of files that it has stored
(and it _can_ bring back a whole dir of committed files).

It never stored anything for the file in **a**, nor for the uncommitted edits in **c**:
there, `git restore` would only give you the last committed version.

</details>

:::

## VS Code's Git functionality

VS Code has built-in Git functionality,
which can be more user-friendly than the Git command-line interface,
especially for showing changes in files.
To have a change to look at, let's first modify the to-do list
you made in Exercise 3.

**Open `todo.txt` in the editor** by clicking on it in the file explorer,
and add a line to it (again, press <kbd>Enter</kbd> at the end of the line):

```{.file filename="todo.txt" .numberLines startFrom="1" hl-lines="2"}
June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
June 20, 1858: Send draft to Huxley


```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

First, in the file explorer, several "decorations" related to Git are shown,
as can be seen in the screenshot on the right:

- Files that have been modified since the last commit are shown in orange and
  marked with an **`M`**.

- The `.gitignore` file has a Git icon next to it.

- Files that are ignored via `.gitignore` are shown in a paler color
  (`data` and `todo.txt~` on the right).

- Untracked files that are _not_ ignored would be shown in green and marked
  with a **`U`** --- there are none here.

2. Then, your editor should show a nice **overview of the changes made** to the file,

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Showing changes on the command line with `git diff` *(Click to expand)*

The `git diff` command also shows changes made to tracked files.
By default, for each file, it shows changes between the **working tree**
and either the last commit or the stage/Index, depending on whether you have staged the file.

So, after the change to the to-do list that you just made,
`git diff` shows the following:

``` sh
git diff
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-bold">diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt
index e3b5e55..9aca508 100644
--- a/todo.txt
+++ b/todo.txt</span>
<span class="git-cyan">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
<span class="git-green">+June 20, 1858: Send draft to Huxley</span></code></pre>

We won't go into the details of the above "diff format",
but at the bottom of the output above, you can see the specific change:
the line "Send draft to Huxley" was added (hence the **`+`** sign) in our
latest version of the file.

Two more notes on `git diff`:

- To show differences between the stage and the last commit,
  use the `--staged` option to `git diff`.
  So, don't be surprised if `git diff` shows nothing right after you ran `git add`!

- If you have changed multiple files, `git diff` will show all of them.
  If you only want to see differences for one of them,
  you can specify the filename to `git diff`.
  In our example, doing so prints the same output as the plain `git diff` command
  above, since we only changed one file:

  ```sh
  git diff todo.txt
  # Output not shown, same as above
  ```
:::

### Staging and committing

Finally, let's commit the change that you made to the to-do list,
now using the Source Control side bar instead of Git commands:

1. Hover over `todo.txt` under **Changes**,
   and click the **`+`** icon that appears to stage the file.
   It should move to a new **Staged Changes** section.

2. Type a commit message in the box at the top of the side bar:
   "Added Huxley draft to to-do list".

3. Click the **Commit** button below the message box.

After that, the side bar should no longer list any changes,
and the number in the version control icon should be gone:
your working tree is "clean" again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Committing this change on the command line instead *(Click to expand)*

The command-line equivalent of what you just did would have been:

``` sh
git add todo.txt
git commit -m "Added Huxley draft to to-do list"
```

Or, with the `-a` option to `git commit`,
which stages and commits changes in tracked files in one step:

``` sh
git commit -am "Added Huxley draft to to-do list"
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### What about the "Publish Branch" button? *(Click to expand)*

At the top of the Source Control side bar,
you may have noticed a blue **Publish Branch** button.
That button creates an online copy of your repo on GitHub in a few clicks.

We will create such an online copy (a "remote" repository) in the
[next lecture](./w5c_github.qmd), but in a different way:
on the GitHub website and with Git commands,
so that you can see each of the steps involved.
The VS Code alternative is explained [in a callout there](./w5c_github.qmd#vscode-publish).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### What am I allowed to use in this course?
In class, we will mostly use the command line for our Git operations.
But it's up to you whether you want to use the command line or the VS Code interface
in your at-home course work, including graded assignments and the final project.
:::

## Self-study: Recap and best practices

### The commands you learned today

| Command               | What it does                                 |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `git init`            | Start a new repo in the current dir          |
| `git status`          | Show which files changed and what is staged  |
| `git add <file>`      | Start tracking a file and stage its changes  |
| `git commit -m "..."` | Save a snapshot of all staged changes        |
| `git log [--oneline]` | Show the commit history                      |
| `git diff`            | Show what changed in tracked files           |
| `git restore <file>`  | Get a file back as it was in the last commit |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[35,65]"}

And remember the `.gitignore` file,
which keeps files you don't want to track out of `git status` output.

### A few Git best practices

Several of these have already been mentioned above,
but here is a summary of some key points:

- **Write informative commit messages.**
  Imagine looking back at your project in a few months,
  after finding an error that you introduced a while ago.
  - Not-so-good commit message: "*Updated file*"
  - Good commit message: "*In file x, updated function y to include z*"

![By XKCD - [image source](https://xkcd.com/1296){target="_blank"}](/img/xkcd-git-commit-msg.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" fig-alt="A humorous cartoon showing ever-worsening Git commit messages over time." .lightbox}

- **Commit often, using small commits.**\
  This will also help to keep commit messages informative!

- **Before committing, check what you've changed.**\
  Use `git diff [--staged]` or VS Code functionality.

- **Avoid including unrelated changes in commits.**\
  Separate commits if your working tree contains work from disparate edits:
  use `git add` + `git commit` separately for two sets of files.

- **Don't commit unnecessary files.**\
  These clutter your repo and its history
  (especially automatically generated, temporary files),
  and when collaborating, they can lead to so-called
  [merge conflicts](../bonus/git.qmd#merge-conflicts).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: File states

Say that in a different repo, `git status` prints the following:

<pre class="bash-out-solo"><code>On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged &lt;file&gt;..." to unstage)
        <span class="git-green">modified:   scripts/qc.sh</span>

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore &lt;file&gt;..." to discard changes in working directory)
        <span class="git-red">modified:   README.md</span>

Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">scripts/trim.sh</span></code></pre>

1. Which file(s) would be included in a commit if you now ran `git commit -m "My message"`?

   a) Only `scripts/qc.sh`
   b) `scripts/qc.sh` and `README.md`
   c) All three files
   d) None of them: you first need to run `git add`

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   The correct answer is **a)**.
   Only _staged_ changes are included in a commit.
   `README.md` was modified but not staged,
   and `scripts/trim.sh` is not even tracked.
   </details>

2. And which file(s) would be included if you instead ran `git commit -am "My message"`
   (see [this box above](#commit-am) for the `-a` option to `git commit`)?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   `scripts/qc.sh` and `README.md`:
   the `-a` option stages all changes to _tracked_ files,
   but it does not add untracked files.
   </details>

3. Say that, before committing, you edit `scripts/qc.sh` once more, without running `git add` on it again.
   How do you think `git status` would list this file,
   and which version of it would `git commit -m "My message"` include?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   `scripts/qc.sh` would be listed twice:
   under "Changes to be committed" _and_ under "Changes not staged for commit".
   `git add` stages the file as it was at that moment,
   so the commit would only include the earlier, staged changes.
   To also include your newest edits, run `git add` on the file again.
   </details>
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
